questions.question: What does the term 'proto-industrialisation' refer to?
options: The phase of space exploration and computer automation
The decline of agriculture and return to hunting-gathering
The establishment of cottage craft shops inside royal palaces
The phase of industrialisation before factories began to appear, characterized by large-scale decentralized production for international markets
questions.explanation: Historians refer to 'proto-industrialisation' as the phase of industrial production prior to modern factories, where goods were produced by peasant households in the countryside for international merchants.

questions.question: Why did merchants from European towns begin moving to the countryside in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries?
options: Towns were completely destroyed by volcanic eruptions
Peasants in villages had invented steam engines
Urban craft and trade guilds were powerful in towns and restricted the entry of new producers
Merchants were legally banished from cities by royal decrees
questions.explanation: In towns, powerful craft guilds maintained monopolies, regulated prices, and restricted new competition. Merchants therefore moved to the countryside, advancing money to poor peasants to produce textiles.

questions.question: In pre-factory England, which city came to be known as the 'finishing centre' where textiles were dyed and finished before export?
options: London
Manchester
Liverpool
Birmingham
questions.explanation: In the proto-industrial network, woollen cloth was sheared, spun, and woven across rural shires, but brought to London for final finishing and dyeing before being exported overseas.

questions.question: Who created the cotton mill, bringing all stages of textile production under one roof under careful supervision?
options: James Hargreaves
Richard Arkwright
James Watt
Matthew Boulton
questions.explanation: Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, bringing spinning, weaving, carding, and rolling under one roof, enabling centralized supervision and quality control.

questions.question: Who invented the Spinning Jenny in 1764, which speeded up spinning by allowing one worker to turn a single wheel and spin multiple threads simultaneously?
options: James Hargreaves
Richard Arkwright
John Kay
Samuel Crompton
questions.explanation: The Spinning Jenny was devised by James Hargreaves in 1764. It revolutionized spinning by turning several spindles with a single wheel, drastically reducing labour demand.

questions.question: Who improved the steam engine originally designed by Newcomen and patented the new efficient model in 1781?
options: Matthew Boulton
George Stephenson
James Watt
Henry Bessemer
questions.explanation: James Watt improved the Newcomen steam engine and patented the new model in 1781. His industrialist partner Matthew Boulton manufactured the new engines.

questions.subtopic: Hand Labour Preference in Victorian Britain
questions.question: Why did many industrialists in Victorian Britain prefer hand labour over expensive machinery?
options: Machinery was legally banned by British Parliament
There was an abundance of poor migrant human labour available at low wages, and many industries had seasonal demand
Electric power had not been invented yet
Workers refused to eat machine-manufactured food
questions.explanation: Britain had an abundant supply of cheap migrant labour. In seasonal trades (breweries, gas works, printing, ship repair), hiring seasonal workers by hand was far more cost-effective than investing large capital in machines.

questions.question: In Victorian Britain, what kind of products did the aristocrats and bourgeoisie prefer to buy as symbols of refinement and social class?
options: Uniform, mass-produced machine goods
Cheap imported plastic goods from colonies
Unrefined raw materials from rural cottage weavers
Handmade goods with intricate individual designs and fine finish
questions.explanation: Handmade goods symbolized refinement and aristocratic taste because they were individually produced, possessed exquisite design, and were carefully finished, unlike uniform mass-produced machine wares.

questions.question: Before the establishment of British colonial rule, which two vibrant Indian ports connected India to the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, and Southeast Asian trade networks?
options: Bombay and Calcutta
Madras and Visakhapatnam
Goa and Cochin
Surat on the Gujarat coast and Hooghly in Bengal
questions.explanation: Surat on the Gujarat coast (linking to the Gulf and Red Sea ports) and Hooghly in Bengal (trading with Southeast Asia) were the premier pre-colonial trade hubs managed by Indian merchants.

questions.question: Who was a 'Gomastha' appointed by the English East India Company in weaving villages?
options: A village school teacher appointed to teach English
A paid servant appointed to supervise weavers, collect supplies, and examine cloth quality
A traditional village priest performing temple rituals
A French diplomatic spy monitoring British troop movements
questions.explanation: The East India Company appointed paid supervisors called 'Gomasthas' to oversee weavers, ensure quality standards, collect woven supplies, and prevent weavers from dealing with other buyers.

questions.question: How did the East India Company prevent Indian weavers from dealing with rival French, Dutch, or Portuguese buyers?
options: By locking all weavers inside fortified cantonments
By confiscating all weaving handlooms across Bengal
By advancing loans to purchase raw materials, which legally obligated weavers to sell exclusively to the Company
By paying weavers wages 10 times higher than European competitors
questions.explanation: Through the system of advances, weavers took loans from the Company to buy raw cotton; once accepted, the advance legally tied the weaver to deliver all woven cloth exclusively to the Company's gomastha.

questions.question: In which year was the first cotton textile mill established in Bombay?
questions.explanation: The first cotton textile mill in India was established in Bombay in 1854, and it went into commercial cloth production in 1856.

questions.question: Where and in which year was the first jute mill established in Bengal?
options: At Howrah in 1870
At Rishra in 1855
At Chittagong in 1890
At Murshidabad in 1845
questions.explanation: The first jute mill was set up at Rishra, near Calcutta on the banks of the Hooghly river, in 1855.

questions.question: Which visionary Indian entrepreneur made a fortune in the China trade and established six joint-stock companies in Bengal in the 1830s and 1840s?
options: Rabindranath Tagore
Debendranath Tagore
Dwarkanath Tagore
Satyendranath Tagore
questions.explanation: Dwarkanath Tagore believed that India would develop through westernisation and industrialisation. He earned wealth in the China trade and set up six joint-stock companies in Bengal.

questions.question: Which Marwari businessman set up the first Indian-owned jute mill in Calcutta in 1917, having made his fortune trading with China?
options: G.D. Birla
Jamsetjee Jeejeebhoy
Purshottamdas Thakurdas
Seth Hukumchand
questions.explanation: In 1917, Seth Hukumchand, a Marwari businessman who traded with China, set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta, breaking European corporate monopoly.

questions.question: In late nineteenth-century Indian mills, who was the 'Jobber'?
options: An old and trusted worker employed by mill owners to recruit new workers from his village
A European technician operating steam engines
A colonial tax collector checking trade licenses
A legal attorney representing trade unions in court
questions.explanation: Industrialists employed a 'Jobber', usually an old and trusted worker, to get new recruits from his village, help them settle in the city, and secure them factory employment.

questions.question: Why did Indian industrial production boom dramatically during the First World War (1914-1918)?
options: The British government transferred all Manchester machinery to Bombay
Electricity was made free of cost for all Indian factories
British mills were busy with wartime production, causing British imports to plunge, while Indian mills were called upon to supply war materials (jute bags, cloth, boots)
Trade with Germany and Austria expanded five-fold
questions.explanation: With British mills preoccupied with war needs, Manchester imports into India dropped steeply. Indian mills stepped in to supply the home market as well as war requirements (uniforms, tents, jute bags).

questions.question: What was the 'fly shuttle', adopted by Indian handloom weavers in the early twentieth century?
options: A small aerocraft used for spraying pesticides on cotton fields
A steam-powered spinning wheel designed for cottage homes
A shuttle train transporting textile workers between Bombay and Thane
A mechanical device operated by ropes and pullies that speeded up weaving and allowed larger looms to be operated by a single weaver
questions.explanation: The fly shuttle was a mechanical weaving device operated by cords and pullies that enabled weavers to operate wider looms at higher speeds, boosting productivity.

questions.question: Why did Manchester textile manufacturers print images of Indian gods and goddesses (like Krishna and Saraswati) on cloth labels sold in India?
options: Because Indian kings owned the factories in Manchester
To make the foreign cloth seem familiar, divine, and spiritually approved by Indian consumers
To comply with compulsory British Christian missionary regulations
Because British artists could only paint Hindu deities
questions.explanation: Images of Hindu gods and goddesses were prominently placed on labels so that foreign-made cloth gained instant consumer trust, appearing as though it had divine approval.

questions.question: During the nationalist struggle, how did Indian manufacturers market their products to compete against foreign goods?
options: By advertising buying Swadeshi products as a patriotic duty for the nation
By selling all goods at zero price
By disguising their goods under British brand names
By printing royal portraits of King George V on labels
questions.explanation: Indian industrialists framed the purchase of Indian manufactured goods as an act of national resistance and patriotic duty: 'If you care for the nation, buy products made in India'.
